title: Understanding GitHub Actions Contexts
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of understanding github actions contexts and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to understanding github actions contexts.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on understanding github actions contexts. Contexts such as `github`, `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `runner`, `job`, `steps`, `needs`, `matrix`, and `inputs` expose different data at different evaluation points. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding GitHub Actions Contexts matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Contexts such as `github`, `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `runner`, `job`, `steps`, `needs`, `matrix`, and `inputs` expose different data at different evaluation points. Contexts, environment variables, and expressions have different scopes and evaluation times. Treat event data as untrusted and avoid interpolating untrusted values directly into shell source. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: The secrets context
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: The runner context
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: The needs context
items.text: Declare job dependencies with `needs` and read prerequisite results or outputs through `needs.<job>`. Separate jobs do not share a runner workspace automatically.

items.title: The matrix and strategy contexts
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Validate input and exit status"
  report:
    needs: validate
    if: ${{ always() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Inspect the dependency result before acting"
content_blocks.expected_output: The reporting job waits for the validation job and runs even after it finishes; real cleanup/reporting logic should inspect `needs.validate.result` before making decisions.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain understanding github actions contexts, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Pass explicit values between workflow components while treating event data as untrusted input.

content.task: Apply understanding github actions contexts to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Contexts such as `github`, `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `runner`, `job`, `steps`, `needs`, `matrix`, and `inputs` expose different data at different evaluation points.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Contexts such as `github`, `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `runner`, `job`, `steps`, `needs`, `matrix`, and `inputs` expose different data at different evaluation points. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
